newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Global telecom pact bid boosted by WTO talks - EU.
newsitem.headline: Global telecom pact bid boosted by WTO talks - EU.

text.p: The European Union said on Thursday that talks this week had won a breakthrough towards a deal to free up the world's $500 billion basic telecommunications market by the deadline of next February 15.

A statement by EU Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan said pledges from several countries seen as vital for a pact -- including Singapore, Egypt, Jamaica and South Africa -- had given new momentum to the on-off negotiations.

"I feel that our discussions have demonstrated a firm political will to bring these negotiations to a successful conclusion and that the Singapore meeting has been a breakthrough event in this process," Brittan declared.

He said he had instructed EU negotiators at World Trade Organisation (WTO) headquarters in Geneva to firm up details of an accord which he now believed was "clearly achievable", especially after the EU-U.S. "infotech" deal in Singapore.

But trade diplomats cautioned that a final accord would still hang on whether the United States -- which walked away from an earlier attempt to reach a pact in April -- was happy with packages put up by Asian countries and also Brazil.

A U.S. official who asked not to be identified was noncommital on how far prospects for a telecoms deal had improved. "We will have to see in February whether there is a good enough critical mass of offers on the table," he said.

In April, the last telecoms bid failed when Washington -- under heavy pressure from U.S. industry -- deemed that a "critical mass" had not been achieved to a degree sufficient to justify it opening up its own market to all comers.

But the talks resumed this autumn and got a boost in November when Washington and Brussels -- earlier at odds on several issues -- put up new packges which they said largely met each other's concerns.

The latest talks were held on the fringes of the 128-member WTO's first ministerial conference, due to end on Friday with a declaration which will commit signatories to achieve "successful conclusion" on telecoms in February.

"In my view, there are now really strong grounds for optimism," said one key figure at the centre of the negotiations -- to resume in Geneva early in the New Year with an intensive effort down the home stretch to begin in mid-January.

Brittan said the infotech, or IT, agreement to remove all tariffs on most information technology products by the year 2000 and joined by many developing countries would give "additional momentum" to the telecom talks.
"Both agreements are essential building blocks to the emerging global information society," he said.
EU negotiator Karl Falkenberg said all the nearly 50 countries in the discussions agreed on their importance.
"The common thread...is that all participants share the perception that telecommunications is a strategic industry and a generator of employment for all our economies," he said.

Trade diplomats said Singapore's announcement on Wednesday that it would now open its domestic market to foreign firms by the year 2000 -- two years earlier than its last offer -- had been widely welcomed.
Brittan said Slovakia had joined Singapore in tabling an "important" offer, and Barbados would be following suit.

Indonesia, a market the United States especially wants to see opened up, had said it is seriously considering making its first offer, while Australia, Canada, Hong Kong, South Korea, Poland and Switzerland promised to improve current offers.
